## What a drill has to prove

Most ear-training apps hand you a number at the end and nothing else. Nine out
of ten. Nine out of ten what, though? If you don't know which intervals came up,
how long you had to answer, or how often the easy ones were drawn, that nine
tells you almost nothing about what you can recognise. Write the drill yourself
and every one of those conditions becomes a line you can read.

Four conditions matter, and the program below makes all four visible. It picks a
root at random from a seeded stream, picks a distance from a pool you control,
leaves a fixed pause for your answer, and only then prints the name and replays
the sound. Prompt before label, always. A label that appears while the notes are
still sounding trains your eyes.

The pool does double duty. It says which intervals are in play, and, because
`choose` samples it uniformly, repeating an entry makes that interval come up
more often. You'll use that to give a weak interval extra trials without
touching the playback loop.

## Ten trials, seeded

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_random_seed 42
use_bpm 72
use_synth :piano

names = {2 => "major second", 4 => "major third", 7 => "perfect fifth", 12 => "octave"}
pool = [2, 4, 7, 12, 7]

10.times do |trial|
  root = rrand_i(note(:c3), note(:b4))
  distance = pool.choose
  play root, release: 0.7
  sleep 1
  play root + distance, release: 0.7
  sleep 4
  puts "trial #{trial + 1}: #{names[distance]}"
  play root; sleep 0.75; play root + distance
  sleep 2
end
```

Each trial gives you an ascending pair somewhere between C3 and B4, then four
beats of silence. At 72 BPM that's a little over three seconds. The name lands
in the log, the pair sounds again, and you get to hear your answer against the
thing you were answering about. That replay is the part most drills leave out,
and it's the part that actually teaches.

Before you run it, guess: across ten trials from that five-item pool, how many
fifths do you expect? Write the number down and compare it with what the log
gives you.

## Tune one condition at a time

1. Add another copy of whichever distance you miss most. Work out its new share
   of the array before you press Run: five entries become six, so a doubled
   interval goes from two in five to two in six for the others and one in three
   for yours. Nothing about how a trial renders has changed.
2. Restore the pool and cut the answer pause from four beats to two. Can you
   still name the sound before the reveal, or have you started answering the
   clock? Those feel identical from the inside, which is why the record matters.
3. Restore the four beats and narrow the roots to a single octave, C4 to B4.
   Run ten trials, then widen the range again and run ten more. Sort your misses
   by distance and see whether recognition was leaning on a familiar register.

## The drill is a small test runner

Look at the shape and it's a structure you already know. `names` is the table of
valid cases and expected results. `pool` defines scope and sampling weight
together. `rrand_i` generates the fixture, the answer pause is the window where
the system under test does its work, and the reveal is the assertion. What makes
this one unusual is that the system under test is you, so the assertion has to
be recorded by hand before the expected value prints.

Weighting by duplication reads clearly at this size. Five slots, two of them
fifths, so fifths arrive twice as often as anything else. Grow the trainer to
twenty intervals and a list of duplicates stops communicating policy, and
explicit counts or probabilities serve you better. Whichever form you pick,
print it at the top of the session. A score that arrives without its sampling
distribution can't explain its own difficulty.

## What the seed buys you, and when it stops

`use_random_seed 42` makes the ten roots and ten distances identical from run to
run, which is what lets you change the answer pause and know that everything
else held still. That guarantee is narrower than it looks. It holds while the
sequence of random calls and the collections they draw from stay the same.

Add a copy to the pool and `choose` samples from a six-element array; every draw
after that point maps differently, and you now have a new session that happens
to be reproducible. Same for changing the root range. Treat those runs as fresh
material and don't compare them trial by trial against the old ones. For
practice you want the opposite of reproducibility: fresh seeds, unfamiliar
roots, material you can't have memorised. Write the seed number down anyway.
When a miss surprises you, that number is what lets you hear it again.

## A score is not evidence on its own

Nine out of ten hides too much. That session might contain no octave at all, or
five fifths because you weighted them. Count three things instead: prompts by
distance, correct answers by distance, and misses by distance. Three small
tallies turn a number into a diagnosis.

When you change the pool, keep the old distribution beside the old score. An
improvement from seven to nine means one thing if the sampling held still and
something quite different if you quietly dropped the interval you kept missing.
Every trainer drifts that way if you let it, because the intervals you enjoy
getting right are the ones you'll keep in the pool.

Per-distance tallies also tell you when a category is really two categories.
Suppose you name every fifth correctly below C4 and half of them above. That
isn't a fifth problem. That's a register problem wearing a fifth's clothing, and
the fix is a wider root range, not more fifths.

The answer pause deserves the same scrutiny as the pool. Too short and you're
measuring reaction time. Too long and each trial turns into a chore, and you'll
do fewer of them. Audition the four-beat value and adjust it until you have room
for a decision and a written answer, with nothing left over.

The distance arrays here also set up the next construction. Lesson 21 arranges
interval steps into a scale formula, turning the same semitone arithmetic from
isolated prompts into an ordered route through a key. Later drills for scales,
chords and cadences reuse this generator, response window, replay and logged
evidence even as their label sets change.

## Run a session and keep the record

Run ten trials from four ascending intervals and write each answer down before
its reveal. Capture the date, the pool, the seed, the ten prompts, your ten
answers, correctness by distance, and the total. Keep a slip of the finger
distinguishable from a genuine miss; those are different failures and they want
different responses.

Draw all ten targets before the session starts and print them at the end. Doing
it that way keeps the random stream in one place, so a later edit to the pause
or the register can't renumber your prompts. Add a fifth interval only after two
consecutive sessions of at least nine out of ten under the same distribution,
and record whether that rule fired. Before you trust any of this as training
data, audition the pause, the replay level and the root range in Sonic Pi 5.
Your record should explain both what got tested and why the pool changed next.
